videos.title: When Fear Hits This Level, Stocks Usually Do THIS
videos.gist: After Friday's drop, the S&P is in a correction and the VIX closed at 35.9. Their six-gauge dashboard says this looks like a sharp AI-stock selloff, not 2008 — but the market usually falls a bit more first, and rates are the risk to watch.

points.title: How far it has fallen
points.text: The S&P peaked on Oct 6 and is 11.6% below that, 33 trading days later. Friday: S&P down 3.7%, Nasdaq 5.3%, chips almost 11%. The Nasdaq 100 is down 19.8%, a hair from a bear market. Semiconductors are down 42% since June. Only consumer staples rose among the 11 S&P sectors.

points.title: Gauges 1 and 2: panic in the options market
points.text: The VIX closed at 35.9, the highest close since the April 2025 tariff crash. Short-term protection is more expensive than 3-month protection (40.7 vs 30.9), which is rare and usually shows up deep in a selloff. Individual investors are 51% bearish, versus a long-run average of about 31%.

points.title: Gauge 3: the selling is narrow
points.text: About a quarter of S&P stocks actually rose on Friday. The damage is in chips and AI, led by Nvidia: Jensen Huang resigned on Nov 12, then the SEC news hit, and the stock fell about 14% on Friday, roughly 47% below its October high. Revenue still beat, and its outlook already assumes no China data-center chip sales.

points.title: Gauges 4 and 5: credit and earnings look calm
points.text: Junk bond spreads are 3.52 points, the high for this year, but well under the 4.61 of April 2025. They've widened only 0.17 of a point, not the 1–2 points seen before 2001 and 2008. S&P earnings grew 32.9% last quarter, forecasts are still being raised, and the index is about 16.5 times next year's earnings, below its 10-year average of 19.1.

points.title: The catch on earnings: AI spending
points.text: Alphabet, Meta and Amazon are spending more than their operating cash (Amazon is about $42B in the red over 12 months). Only Microsoft still covers its bill. Cloud revenue is still growing fast. If that spending stops paying off, they say this gauge breaks first, when earnings forecasts get cut.

points.title: Gauge 6: rates are stressed
points.text: The Fed already hiked in September to 3.75–4%, inflation is 3.7%, and it meets again on Dec 9. After Friday the market still priced about a 92% chance of another hike, with rates peaking around 4.5%. The 10-year yield is 4.91%, down from 5.31% in early October. Oil is still near $90, and a new Congress plus a Jan 10 trade-truce deadline add political risk. Higher rates hit every stock, not just AI.

points.title: What usually happens after a VIX close above 35
points.text: Since 1990 they found 17 similar first spikes. Six months later the S&P was higher 15 times; a year later, 14 times, with a median gain of 21.6% versus 11.9% in an average year. That is not a bottom call. After those days the S&P usually fell more first (median about 6%). The three misses were 2001, 2008 and March 2022.

points.title: Their read, and what would change it
points.text: This looks more like a sharp correction in AI stocks than the start of 2008: fear is in options, not in credit or earnings. The warning light that matches a bad case is rates (like 2022). Watch for junk spreads above about 4.5 points, earnings forecasts getting cut, or a Dec 9 hike plus a 10-year yield back above 5.25%.

todo: Don't treat a high VIX as a buy-the-bottom signal; in their past cases the S&P usually fell about 6% more first
Watch junk bond spreads; a move above about 4.5 points would mean lenders are backing off
Watch whether analysts start cutting earnings forecasts, especially if AI spending stops paying off
Mark the calendar: Dec 1 Huang's testimony, Dec 9 Fed, Dec 10 inflation report, Jan 10 trade truce
videos.watch: A small channel with its own six-gauge dashboard, not advice. They used 17 cases and picked 35 as a round VIX cutoff; returns are price-only, no dividends. Nvidia and SEC details are from news reports they cite. The next few dates can change the picture fast.

videos.title: The Government is DESPERATE for You to Start This Business
videos.gist: The government already pays small businesses million-dollar contracts for ordinary work. He says the winners research early on SAM.gov and USAspending.gov. They don't wait for an RFP and fire off proposals.

points.title: Five real small-business awards
points.text: Tree maintenance ($1.76M), fire alarm upgrades ($690K, about $510M a year in spend), kosher/halal food for federal prisons ($1M), hospital wandering-protection alarms (about $150M a year), and an $18M airplane hangar repair.

points.title: Don't chase RFPs
points.text: Writing proposals on SAM.gov is the last step. He says companies that only do that rarely win.

points.title: Research past awards first
points.text: On USAspending.gov, look up your NAICS or keywords. See yearly spend, which agencies buy, which states get the work, and who already wins.

points.title: Answer Sources Sought early
points.text: These are questions, not bids. Send your capability statement and recommendations before the solicitation comes out. If you can't do the whole job, look for a teammate or a subcontract.

points.title: Check procurement forecasts
points.text: Acquisition.gov and the Navy long-range forecast list upcoming work, dollar ranges, incumbents, a contracting contact, and the target quarter. Funding can still change.

points.title: For Penguin Air
points.text: You don't have to learn all of government contracting. Just how the government buys HVAC and plumbing. Start with facilities and mechanical work near bases and federal buildings in the Carolinas.

todo: Search USAspending.gov for HVAC, plumbing and facilities maintenance spend near NC
On SAM.gov, filter Sources Sought for mechanical, HVAC and plumbing work
Note bonding, licenses, past performance and base-access requirements before you reply
Check Acquisition.gov forecasts (and nearby DoD ones) for upcoming facilities jobs
If a Sources Sought is bigger than you can do alone, find a teammate or offer to subcontract
videos.watch: This is also a pitch for his paid GovClose program. The dollar figures are his read of public data and they change. No contract is guaranteed.

videos.title: Build Your Own AI Chief of Staff in 6 Steps
videos.gist: You don't need your own AI model. Connect the right pieces and you get an assistant that knows your business and does tasks for you.

points.title: 1. Give it a home
points.text: A computer or cloud server that runs 24/7. He prefers the cloud.

points.title: 2. Install an agentic harness
points.text: Tools so it can click, type and run tasks. He uses Hermes.

points.title: 3. Choose its AI brain
points.text: Claude, ChatGPT or an open-source model.

points.title: 4. Teach it who you are
points.text: Let it interview you about your business, offers, clients and goals.

points.title: 5. Give it a persistent memory
points.text: A second brain tied to your files, contacts and key info.

points.title: 6. Add skills
points.text: Explain a job once. It remembers and repeats it every day.

todo: Pick a home that runs 24/7 (a cloud server is easiest)
Install an agent harness that can click, type and run tasks
Choose the AI model that powers it
Let it interview you about your business, offers, clients and goals
Connect its memory to your files, contacts and key info
Teach it one job at a time as a saved skill
videos.watch: Lead-magnet reel: 'comment JARVIS' gets you his guide. 'One weekend' is his claim. Hermes is his pick, not a tested comparison. Be careful what files and accounts you connect.

videos.title: How to Run Your Own Private AI
videos.gist: You can run AI on hardware you control so files never go to OpenAI or Anthropic. He shows a solo Mac setup and a team server, then how to chat with your documents and lock it down.

points.title: 1. Pick a model with the memory rule
points.text: Size in billions × about 0.6 = GB needed, then leave room for the chat and other apps. A 9B model needs about 7 GB (fine on a 16 GB Mac). A ~30B model needs about 20 GB (32–64 GB RAM). 128 GB can run OpenAI's GPT-OSS 120B. His picks: Qwen 3 9B, then a larger Qwen 3 mixture-of-experts that only uses about 3B per word.

points.title: 2. Solo path: your own Mac (most private)
points.text: Easiest: LM Studio. No terminal. Search a model, download it, load it, drag in a PDF and ask. Full setup: Ollama runs the model (install from ollama.com), Open WebUI is the chat screen (Docker Desktop, then open localhost:3000). Raise Ollama's context length to 16K, and turn Cloud off so models don't run on their servers.

points.title: 3. Team path: a private Ubuntu server
points.text: Plain Ubuntu, no ready-made template. Official install scripts for Ollama, Docker, Open WebUI and Docling. Example he used: Hostinger KVM, 8 cores and 32 GB, about $26/month on the 2-year promo and about $50 at renewal. No graphics card, so it's slow (a few words a second). If 32 GB struggles, drop to the 9B model.

points.title: 4. Put it on your domain with Caddy
points.text: One DNS record, one Caddy install, HTTPS that renews itself. Create the first account right away — it becomes the admin. On a CPU box, turn thinking mode off or it adds a lot of waiting. No domain? Use Tailscale instead.

points.title: 5. Chat with company documents (RAG)
points.text: In Open WebUI, fix document settings before you upload anything (changing them later means reprocessing). Set the embedding model, turn on hybrid search so names and invoice numbers match, and point scanned PDFs at Docling or uploads fail. Create a Knowledge collection, then type # in a chat and pick it. Answers show citations to the exact paragraph.

points.title: 6. Lock it down, in this order
points.text: 2FA on the hosting account. SSH keys, then password login off. Firewall with only ports 22, 80 and 443 open. Never open Ollama's port 11434 — it has no password. Keep software updated. Turn new sign-ups off and add people yourself. Open WebUI has no built-in 2FA, so use Google or Microsoft login, or put it on Tailscale so only your team can see it. Snapshot before every update.

points.title: 7. The honest limits
points.text: A rented server is still someone else's computer. Hostinger's terms say it's not a HIPAA or payment-card environment, so no patient data and no card numbers. Running it yourself doesn't make you compliant — it makes you responsible. Most private option: a machine in your own office with disk encryption on.

points.title: 8. Add n8n for real work
points.text: Install n8n on the same server with one more Docker command and its own Caddy address. Don't use the host's n8n template — a new template can wipe the server. Point n8n at your Ollama model. Then you can pull dates out of a contract uploaded through a form, sort tickets and draft replies, or write a Monday report, and the AI never leaves the server.

points.title: Tools and cost
points.text: LM Studio or Ollama, Docker, Open WebUI, Docling, Caddy, optional Tailscale and n8n. A server is about $26–$50 a month. A 64 GB Mac Mini is a one-time cost, a little under $3,000. A rented graphics card full-time is about $250–$500 a month. Hourly GPU boxes (from about 40 cents/hour) have no backups and get deleted if credit hits zero — don't keep the company brain there.

points.title: Common mistakes
points.text: Don't leave Ollama open to the internet. Researchers found about 17,500 exposed servers; a flaw called Bleeding Llama could leak conversations. Don't upload files before fixing document settings. Delete old policy versions or it will quote the wrong one. Spreadsheets are a trap: search only pulls a few rows, so keep Excel for totals.

todo: Decide solo (your own Mac, most private) vs a team server
If solo: install LM Studio, pick a model that fits your RAM, and drag in a test PDF
If a server: use plain Ubuntu and official install commands — don't use a host template that can wipe the box
In Open WebUI, set embedding, hybrid search and Docling before you upload any files
Lock it down: 2FA, SSH keys, firewall on 22/80/443 only, never open port 11434, turn sign-ups off
Keep customer or card data off a rented VPS. If it has to stay private, use a machine in the office with disk encryption
videos.watch: He also pitches his paid community; exact commands are in a free blog post linked from his profile. A rented VPS is still someone else's computer, and Hostinger says it's not a HIPAA or card-data setup. Captions were messy on some model names (Qwen 3 9B and a larger Qwen 3 mixture-of-experts).

videos.title: Get Unstuck and Get More Done: 9 Principles
videos.gist: Being stuck is a clarity problem, not laziness. Get clear, calm down, then take the next small step.

points.title: Clarity, not laziness
points.text: Not acting means you lost sight of what, how or why.

points.title: What game am I playing?
points.text: Tie each dull task to your bigger vision.

points.title: Find the fear
points.text: Ask: what am I afraid of that makes this hard?

points.title: Morning brain dump
points.text: 3 columns: negative belief, its opposite, evidence it's true.

points.title: The next 10 feet
points.text: Act on the clarity you have. Confidence comes after.

points.title: No escape hatch
points.text: Find a reason big enough that not acting isn't an option.

points.title: Recommit, don't beat yourself up
points.text: See what led to the slip, then recommit for 24 hours.

points.title: Calm before you push
points.text: Action from stress makes more stress. Shift your state first.

points.title: Journal by hand
points.text: 10–15 minutes: thank, ask for what you want, ask for others.

todo: Make a sheet with 3 columns
Column 1: every negative belief you woke up with
Column 2: the exact opposite, written as a new decision
Column 3: evidence the new decision is true (ask 3 times)
Do 2–4 beliefs a morning, for about 30 days
videos.watch: Built from 7 podcast episodes. 3 were the closest match to the YouTube titles.

videos.title: Sales Objection Replies (Nick Ayala Shorts)
videos.gist: Whoever is explaining is losing. Agree, ask one question, then stop talking.

points.title: “Too expensive” / lowball
points.text: Repeat their number slowly and go quiet. Then: “Help me understand how you got to that.”

points.title: Discount request
points.text: “I can work with you on price. Which part of the work should we take out?”

points.title: “Competitor is cheaper”
points.text: “They might be. Can I ask what's included in their number?”

points.title: “No budget right now”
points.text: “If budget wasn't an issue, would this be a yes?” Then wait.

points.title: “Send me a proposal”
points.text: “Before I write it, what needs to be in there for this to be a yes?”

points.title: “Run it by my partner”
points.text: “What do you think they'll ask you?” Then offer to join that call.

points.title: “We went with someone else”
points.text: “What did they do that I didn't?” and “Can I check back in 90 days?”

todo: Write the key lines down before sales calls
Rehearse them out loud
Run the role-plays in the Notion playbook
After each line, stop talking and let them answer
